[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Comprehensive Guide to Categorical Encoding Techniques in Machine Learning"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Most machine learning algorithms require numerical input data. When working with datasets that contain categorical variables, whether nominal (no intrinsic ordering) or ordinal (logical ordering), you must transform these text values into numerical representations. This process is known as categorical encoding."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. One-Hot Encoding"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"One-Hot Encoding creates binary columns for each category present in the feature. If a category is present, its column value is 1, otherwise it is 0. This technique is ideal for nominal data where no ordinal relationship exists."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

# Sample data
df = pd.DataFrame({'City': ['New York', 'London', 'Paris', 'London']})

# Apply One-Hot Encoding using pandas
encoded_df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['City'])
print(encoded_df)"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Label Encoding"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Label Encoding maps each category to an integer value ranging from 0 to n_classes minus one. While efficient, it introduces an implicit numerical ordering (e.g., 2 is greater than 1), which can mislead models if applied to purely nominal features."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

# Sample data
encoder = LabelEncoder()
df['City_Encoded'] = encoder.fit_transform(['New York', 'London', 'Paris', 'London'])
print(df)"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Ordinal Encoding"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ordinal Encoding is similar to Label Encoding, but it allows you to explicitly define the ranking order of the categories. This is particularly useful for features like education level (High School < Bachelor < Master < PhD)."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"from sklearn.preprocessing import OrdinalEncoder

# Sample data with explicit order
df = pd.DataFrame({'Education': ['Bachelor', 'PhD', 'High School', 'Master']})
encoder = OrdinalEncoder(categories=[['High School', 'Bachelor', 'Master', 'PhD']])
df['Education_Ordinal'] = encoder.fit_transform(df[['Education']])
print(df)"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Target Encoding (Mean Encoding)"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Target Encoding replaces each category with the average target value for that category. It is highly effective for high-cardinality categorical variables, though precautions against data leakage and overfitting must be taken."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use One-Hot Encoding for nominal variables with low cardinality."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Ordinal Encoding when categories possess a clear hierarchical ranking."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use Target Encoding cautiously for high-cardinality nominal features, ensuring proper cross-validation."}]
